visits.text: From Manambato, embark on the Pangalanes Canal - 665 km of waterway running along the east coast, laid out by General Gallieni. Vanilla, coffee and clove plantations line the banks; merchant pirogues still use it daily. The journey to Akanin'ny Nofy takes 1.5 hours: watch local life unfold from the boat.

The Palmarium reserve, on the shores of Lake Ampitabe, is home to about ten species of lemurs living semi-free - some very tame ones come within arm's reach. Do not feed them. The flora is just as remarkable: orchids, carnivorous plants, extremely rare endemic palms including Voanioala and Lemurophoenix.

Cross Lake Ampitabe by boat to visit a Betsimisaraka village on the opposite shore. No staging - just a direct encounter with a community living off fishing and rice, cut off from the rest of the world by water. Take time for a meal on site if you're invited.

activities.text: Night boat outing to Île au Coq to observe the Aye-Aye - this very rare nocturnal lemur accumulates oddities: bat ears, skeletal fingers including one very long one for extracting larvae from trunks, hallucinated stare. Departure around 5:30pm, duration about 1 hour. Arrange through your accommodation.
Free day on the lakeshore - swimming from the white sand beach, kayaking, hammock or walk through the coastal forest. Akanin'ny Nofy means "nest of dreams" in Malagasy: that's exactly it.

visits.text: 12 km south of Ambalavao on the RN7, stop at Anja reserve - managed directly by villagers since 1999, no national park or large structure. They protect around 400 ring-tailed lemurs here, the ones with the long black-and-white striped tail. Arrive early: in the morning, the makis are active and unafraid - they sometimes approach within a meter. The profits have funded a village school. Allow 2 hours for the small loop.

Stop by an Antemoro paper workshop in Ambalavao - they make pulp from the bark of the avoha shrub, embedding dried flowers and leaves. The result resembles floral parchment. You can watch every step and leave with sheets made on site.

If you're there on a Wednesday, don't miss the zebu market - 2,000 head of cattle transit through this town every week. The herders draped in colorful blankets, the bargaining ritual and the auctions are a spectacle in themselves.

activities.text: Guided circuit in Anja reserve - the local guide will also show you chameleons, boas and endemic birds tucked among the rocks that you'd never have spotted alone.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island
Madagascar's Highlands: Culture, Crafts and Forests Along the RN7

visits.text: Push open the door to a workshop in Ambositra - you're entering the world of the Zafimaniry, whose woodcraft is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. No nails, no screws: panels carved with geometric motifs fit together by hand, following rules transmitted orally from father to son for centuries. The same motifs cover walls, doors and furniture of houses - it's a visual language.

If you have time, take the track to the village of Antoetra, allowing a full day for the round trip from Ambositra - there you will see Zafimaniry work in its real setting, in a real house, with the real tools. Not in a tourist shop.

activities.text: Browse Ambositra's craft markets and buy directly from producers - marquetry, wood carvings, textiles. Prices are well below Tana's for the same pieces.

visits.text: Stop at Marozevo on the road from Tana to visit the Peyrieras reserve - a breeding center for giant butterflies, chameleons and endemic frogs. Takes 45 minutes and provides good preparation for the Andasibe forest.

In Andasibe, enter the Analamazaotra reserve at opening with your local guide - mandatory and essential. You're here for the indri-indri: the world's largest lemur, 70 cm, 7 kg, capable of jumping 10 meters from tree to tree. Its call - deep and powerful, carrying several kilometers - awakens the forest at dawn. If you hear it before seeing it, follow the sound. The forest also shelters 11 other lemur species and extremely rare Eulophiella orchids.

activities.text: Night forest walk by flashlight - sportive and mouse lemurs with shining eyes in the branches. Arrange the outing the same morning at the park entrance or through your accommodation.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island

visits.text: Allow roughly 2 hours of driving to reach the ochre canyon of the Red Tsingy of Irodo, 60 km south of Diego on the RN6. This site resembles nothing else in Madagascar: unlike the limestone tsingy of Ankarana, these formations are sculpted from red sandstone, marl, and laterite by erosion from the Irodo River and rain. Hundreds of fairy chimneys range in shade from white to blood red, and the late-afternoon light sets them ablaze—and since the site is ephemeral, each rainy season reshapes the sculptures. Two viewpoints accessible by car overlook the canyon; a third access route leads down on foot to the base of the formations. Bring water and a hat.

Continuing south on the RN6, the landscape gradually shifts: the red laterite gives way to the first gray limestone formations and dry deciduous forests that herald the Ankarana massif. The “Ankarana wall,” a limestone cliff stretching 25 km from north to south, looms on the horizon—it's a geological transition visible to the naked eye, two worlds separated by a few dozen kilometers.

The Ankarana Special Reserve (18,220 ha, created in 1956, UNESCO-listed in September 2023) shelters Africa's largest cave network: 110 km of underground cavities carved into Jurassic limestone that emerged from the seas 100 million years ago. Above ground, the tsingy—the Malagasy word means 'walking on tiptoes'—form a labyrinth of razor-sharp limestone pinnacles, deep canyons, and crevasses. Stop at the Mahamasina reception office before entering—a guide is mandatory. The site is 108 km south of Antsiranana.
The Perte des Rivières is one of Ankarana's most spectacular phenomena: a river with green waters briefly crosses a canyon before disappearing beneath the rock to join the underground network.

Two suspension bridges connect the viewpoints above the great canyon of the Benavony loop, offering a plunging view over the stone forest and crevasses. From the high point at 206 m, on clear days you glimpse the islets of the Mozambique Channel. A great baobab 8 m in circumference awaits you at the circuit's end. Ankarana's dry forest shelters three endemic baobab species: Adansonia madagascariensis, Adansonia perrieri, and Adansonia suarezensis.

activities.text: Visiting the Red Tsingy is largely done by car between viewpoints. To descend into the heart of the fairy chimneys, count on 45 minutes on foot from the third access. The best light is late afternoon: if your timing allows, organize your departure from Diego to arrive on site around 4 PM.

Eight circuits are marked in the reserve, ranging from 3 km to 10 km and from 2 hours to a full day. The Benavony loop (5 km, 3 to 4 hours) is the most comprehensive: tsingy, two suspension bridges, a cave with mineral formations, and a panoramic viewpoint. For the Perte des Rivières (4 km, 3 hours), bring shoes that can get wet. Pack a headlamp for the caves.

Some Ankarana caves shelter the royal tombs of the Antakarana, who took refuge in the massif in the 19th century to flee Merina armies. These caves are sacred, and Merina descendants are forbidden from entering them—a history of conflicts between Malagasy kingdoms that remains very much alive in local memory. Ask your guide to tell you this story along the way.

places.name: Antananarivo

visits.text: Head up to Rova Manjakamiadana first thing in the morning - perched 200 metres above Tana on Analamanga hill, it's the only spot where you can take in the entire capital in a single sweep. Jean Laborde, a French adventurer, clad it in stone between 1839 and 1841 for Queen Ranavalona I; a 1995 fire gutted the interiors, which have since been restored and reopened. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes - and ignore the hawkers at the entrance.

The Upper Town (Tanàna Ambony) is designated a protected area of historical interest. Its sloping cobbled lanes, red-brick houses and cascading stairways look like a European old-town neighbourhood catapulted into the Indian Ocean. Climb up to the viewpoint in the late afternoon: the golden light on the rooftops is worth the detour.
Take a look around Andravoahangy market. Spices, silver filigree jewellery, spare parts, live poultry. Go in the morning before 10 a.m., when the stalls are full.

Make the drive to Ambohimanga, 21 km north of Tana - allow an hour in traffic. This isn't your average tourist site: Malagasy people still come here on pilgrimage to make wishes. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, the royal city is sealed by a 12-tonne stone disc. The Mahandrihono palace, built of rosewood, was home to King Andrianampoinimerina - the one who dreamed of a kingdom bounded only by the sea.

At Ambohimanga, look at the rosewood Mahandrihono palace and the gate closed by a stone disc: these features offer a tangible introduction to the royal city. Do not point at sacred sites: bend your index finger, as local people will explain.

At the end of the day, step into the Museum of Art and Archaeology in the Isoraka neighbourhood in Tana - collections of beads, ceramics and ritual objects that tell Madagascar's story better than any guide. Often empty of tourists, which is a bonus.

Back to Tana - use the drive to observe the terraced rice paddies of the highlands from the road. On arrival, step into the Musée de l'Académie Malgache in the Ambohijatovo neighbourhood. The collections of manuscripts, traditional musical instruments and old maps of Madagascar are presented without frills - that's precisely what makes them credible.

Late afternoon, return to Andravoahangy market for your last purchases - silver jewellery vendors are particularly numerous late in the day. Don't leave without a hand-worked filigree silver souvenir.

Last day in Tana. If you have a few hours before your flight, take a look around the Digue craft market - silver jewellery, zebu-horn lamps, embroidery, basketry. It is your last chance to leave with something made in Madagascar rather than imported.

For the curious, Tsarasaotra park, an ornithological reserve right in the city, is home to ducks, herons and other endemic birds a few kilometres from the centre. Half an hour is enough and it's completely unexpected in a capital city.

activities.text: Wander the lanes of the Upper Town on foot in early evening - locals heading home, children playing on the stairs, colonial houses lighting their windows. The best time to feel Tana's rhythm without a guide.

Walk the trail through the remaining forest around Ambohimanga's Rova - one of the last fragments of primary deciduous forest in inland Madagascar. The local guide will explain the traditional uses of endemic plant species.

A return stroll through the Isoraka neighbourhood in the evening - craft shops, restaurants and small local bars rub shoulders here, in a neighbourhood more relaxed than the Upper Town. This is where expats and travellers at the end of their circuit meet up.
Departure for Ivato airport - allow a minimum of 1 hour 30 minutes from the centre, 2 hours at rush hour. Tana traffic is unpredictable.

visits.text: Welcome to Antsirabe - the town that smells of sulphur and minerals. Perched at 1,500 m on a volcanic plateau, it draws its thermal water from ground so salt-laden it earned the nickname “where there's a lot of salt”. Its colonial avenues swarm with brightly painted pousse-pousse - hop into one to cross town: it's the quintessential local transport.

Lake Tritriva is worth the detour: plan a round trip along a dirt track during the day from Antsirabe. This volcanic crater, 160 metres deep and filled with dark blue-green water, is sacred. Do not eat pork before going - villagers strongly advise against it, and the legend of a tourist who drowned after ignoring this taboo still circulates. Seen from above, the lake has exactly the shape of Madagascar. Allow 20 minutes to walk around it.

On the way, stop at Lake Andraikiba, 7 km from town - more accessible and livelier: fishermen striking the water with bundles of sticks to stun the fish, women washing clothes on the banks. A peaceful spot to catch your breath.

Stop in front of Antsirabe's colonial railway station and look at its ochre façade. The building is worth viewing from outside, even without much rail activity. Continue on foot through the streets behind the station to explore the surrounding neighbourhoods and their colourful rickshaws. This walk stays within the town for this stage of the itinerary and does not depend on a market day.

Antsirabe's colonial railway station is a handsome ochre building constructed under French administration, which served as the starting point for the line heading south. It hasn't seen much traffic for a long time, but the building itself warrants a stop.

activities.text: Visit a semi-precious stone workshop in central Antsirabe - the artisans work in front of you and sell directly, at prices far lower than in Tana. Antsirabe is known across the island for its surrounding quarries.
Take a pousse-pousse ride through the town centre streets - negotiate directly with the driver. It's a concrete way to support the local economy.
Visit a zebu-horn workshop - Antsirabe's craftspeople cut and polish the horn to make jewellery, combs and decorative objects. Buy directly from the workshop.
Take one last pousse-pousse ride through the lanes behind the station - the neighbourhoods outside the centre are less visited and more authentic.

visits.text: Sakalava Bay is your starting point for the Three Bays hike. Reach it from Diego via a 5 km sandy track from the Ankorikely junction—you'll need a 4x4, as not all regular taxis go there. The bay is hammered by the Varatraza trade winds, making it one of the country's best kitesurfing spots. Set off early: the heat quickly becomes intense after 10 AM on this shadeless coastline.

Between Sakalava Bay and Pigeons Bay, you walk alongside dunes and drought-adapted vegetation typical of the north—pachypodiums and dryland species growing between sand ridges. Dunes Bay offers a swimming break in crystal-clear waters with few visitors. From the blockhouse overlooking it, you can see both bays at once—stop for a photo.

Pigeons Bay marks the northern end of the hike, with whiter sand and a more sheltered sea than Sakalava. This is where the water is calmest—perfect for a final swim before heading back up to the lighthouse. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours of walking in total from Sakalava, depending on your pace.

At Cap Miné, you reach the remains of French fortifications built from 1894 onwards to defend the main channel into Diego Suarez Bay. Four period cannons still stand in place, and the lighthouse first lit on October 1, 1900, remains active. The view from this promontory over the bay and the channel is the region's finest—here you understand why the French navy valued this anchorage so highly. Heads up: the military collect a passage fee at the exit toward Ramena.

activities.text: The Three Bays coastal hike covers about 11 km from Sakalava to Ramena, with moderate elevation changes and some ridge trail sections. Bring plenty of water, a hat, and sunscreen—there's no shade on the ridges. From Ramena, a taxi takes you back to Diego via 18 km of paved road.

From Ramena late in the day, local operators offer short pirogue or boat trips to the Emerald Sea, a natural lagoon with shallow, translucent waters protected by a barrier reef. A mask and snorkel are all you need—you can still touch the bottom for dozens of meters.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Madagascar Road Trip: Tsingy, Three Bays & Nosy Be

visits.text: The sandy track from Morondava to Belo-sur-Mer takes about 5 hours by 4x4 - it crosses baobab forests, fords and nameless villages off the map. Leave at dawn: the track heats up fast and fords are more passable early morning.

In Belo-sur-Mer, head straight to the beachside shipyards. Marine carpenters assemble dhows and pirogues the old way - no plans, no machines, by hand and eye, with local timber. Stay a while and watch them work without asking anything.

This second day in Belo-sur-Mer is the circuit's real luxury - you're not required to go anywhere. Wander the quay at sunrise, watch dhows leave for the day, chat with pirogue builders. The village has no set program. That's its charm.

activities.text: Sailing pirogue outing on the lagoon late afternoon - the waters are turquoise and calm, fishermen returning with their catch. A local operator will take you for a few thousand ariary.
Pirogue excursion to Andravoho island to explore the lagoon's seabed - corals, tropical fish and calm waters. Arrange the outing with your host the evening before.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island
Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island

visits.text: Climb into Fianarantsoa's upper town in the late afternoon - its red-brick lanes stacked across several hills are a listed protected area. Go up to the top viewpoint: the view over the terraced rice fields tumbling down to the valley is one of the finest in the highlands. Wear good shoes - the cobbles are slippery after rain.

Don't leave without tasting the local wine, produced on the surrounding slopes. The red and the white have a very distinctive profile, far from European standards: that is exactly what makes them interesting. Look for the wine cellar in town.

activities.text: Stroll the upper town's lanes in the evening when raking light colors the red bricks and schoolkids head home. It's free, quiet and a hundred times truer than any guided tour.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island
Madagascar's Highlands: Culture, Crafts and Forests Along the RN7

visits.text: Ifaty marks the end of the RN7 - and the beginning of the sea. Forty kilometers north of Tuléar, its white sand beaches are protected by a coral reef that calms coastal waters. After days on the road and track, head straight to the beach upon arrival: cold water on tired legs is the best reward the west coast can offer.

Very early in the morning, watch the Vezo fishermen's pirogues return with their night's catch. This nomadic sea people build their outrigger pirogues on site, right on the sand. Don't miss the improvised shipyards at the beach's edge.

activities.text: Snorkeling on the Ifaty coral reef. Local operators offer mask and snorkel or pirogue trips out to the coral heads.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island

places.name: Ile Aux Nattes

visits.text: Take a pirogue from southern Sainte-Marie - 10 minutes and 400 meters of sea separate the two islands. Île aux Nattes measures 2.5 km by 1.5 km: no cars, trails through coconut palms, a white sand beach at trail's end. After three weeks on the road, settle in and do nothing. That's the objective.
The island's small lemur park shelters ring-tailed makis in forest and some specimens of Eulophiella roempleriana - the giant endemic orchid. A quiet visit, no crowds, no program.

activities.text: Walk around the island - allow 2 hours taking your time on interior trails. You'll encounter three residents, two chickens and a chameleon.
Snorkeling in the lagoon south of the island - crystal-clear water and well-preserved coral reefs. Borrow or bring a mask and snorkel.

days_plan.itin_title: Classic Madagascar Grand Tour: RN7, Baobabs, Pangalanes & Sainte-Marie Island

map_keywords: Island of Palms Nosy Nanto Pirogue
White Sand Beach Island of Palms Snorkeling

visits.text: Upon arrival in Sainte-Marie, start with Ambodifotatra, the main village - its markets, old church and slow, francophone atmosphere set the tone. Sainte-Marie measures 49 km long by 5 km wide: there's no possible rush here.

Visit the pirate cemetery in the Baie des Forbans - reachable on foot at low tide, by pirogue at high tide. Tombstones from the 1830s, some carved with a classic skull, recall that buccaneers made this island their lair between 1680 and 1720.

If you're here between July and September, don't miss the humpback whales - they migrate from Antarctica, 5,000 km, to breed in the Sainte-Marie channel. Peak is in August: 198 individuals were counted in 12 hours from shore during one census. Off season, head to the natural pools of Ambodiatafana in the island's north: granite rocks form basins filled by tides, perfect for swimming.
Make a detour through the Ikalalao forest (400 ha) - three endemic lemur species, chameleons and Eulophiella roempleriana, the giant orchid nicknamed the Queen of Madagascar.

activities.text: Ferry crossing from Soanierana-Ivongo - reconfirm schedules the day before. The Gasikara Be can be cancelled due to swells: always keep flexibility around this crossing. In case of cancellation, short flights from Tamatave or Tana exist as alternatives.

Boat outing for whale watching (July-September) - choose a local operator who respects regulatory distances. Don't dive from the boat near them. Off season, go coastline cruising on the west coast by pirogue instead.

places.name: Iranja

visits.text: Nosy Iranja is actually two islands connected by a 1.2 km white sand tombolo—at low tide, you walk between two turquoise oceans on this tongue of sand that completely disappears at high tide. The large island, Nosy Iranja Be (200 ha), shelters a fishing village and a lighthouse built in 1909 by Gustave Eiffel's workshop, still visible from offshore. The small one, Nosy Iranja Kely (13 ha), is Madagascar's main hawksbill turtle nesting site.

The fishing village of Nosy Iranja Be is worth a stroll: stilt houses built with mangrove wood and traveler's palm leaves, small grocery stores, fruit and fritter stands. Head up to the Eiffel lighthouse (20 m, 1909) for a 360° view over both islets and the tombolo—this is where Nosy Iranja's most famous photo was taken.

The second day at Nosy Iranja is your chance to enjoy the tombolo without the crowds of day-trippers, who leave around 3 PM. At low tide, you have the tongue of sand to yourself in the late afternoon and at sunrise. Nosy Iranja Kely, the small 13-ha island, can be crossed on foot in about twenty minutes through ferns and endemic species.

activities.text: The boat trip from Madirokely to Nosy Iranja takes 1.5 to 2 hours depending on conditions. Leave early in the morning to arrive at low tide and walk along the tombolo as soon as you arrive. Your camping gear awaits you on the island—you won't have to reload anything onto a boat tonight.

Snorkeling just off Nosy Iranja Kely: reefs teeming with fish, turtles at the surface and, in season (July–October), humpback whales spotted offshore. The water is between 27 and 29°C all year round. In the evening, if you are camping overnight, local operators organize nighttime outings to watch turtles laying eggs on the beach of Nosy Iranja Kely—a rare experience.

It is possible to watch hatchlings emerging and heading to the sea at sunrise—the island's most moving moment. Ask your operator to let you know if hatching is underway: it is unpredictable depending on the season but frequent between October and February.

Snorkel independently on the reefs on the west side of Nosy Iranja Kely, where there is no tourist pressure once the boats have left. Enjoy the second day's calm to explore at your own pace—that's the advantage of camping overnight over a day trip.
A late-afternoon walk along the tombolo at sunset. The low-angle light on the white sand and turquoise waters is the day's most photogenic. Check the tide to be sure the tombolo is still exposed.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Madagascar Road Trip: Tsingy, Three Bays & Nosy Be

map_keywords: Tombolo Nosy Iranja banc de sable

visits.text: Amber Mountain National Park is an anomaly in this arid north: an 18,200-hectare volcanic massif perched between 850 and 1,475 meters elevation that receives 3,500 mm of annual rainfall while Diego Suarez gets 1,000 mm. The result—a dense, cool cloud forest draped in orchids, tree ferns, and lianas, in total contrast to the surrounding dry savannas. Created in 1958, the park shelters 8 lemur species including the crowned lemur (Eulemur coronatus) and the rufous mouse lemur, one of the world's smallest primates. Arrive at the entrance office in Joffreville by 7 AM—guides are mandatory and the early hours are best for wildlife watching.

The Thousand Trees Trail crosses the park's rainforest alongside century-old trees draped in lianas and epiphytes. This circuit gives you the best chance of encountering Brookesia tuberculata, one of the planet's tiniest chameleons at under 5 cm. Your guide will spot it in the vegetation—observe and photograph, but don't touch. Furcifer timoni and Calumma vencesi, two recently scientifically described species, also live here.

The great Antomboka waterfall plunges 80 meters through the heart of the forest—it's one of the park's highlights, at the end of a 3 to 4-hour circuit from the entrance. Some routes also include the sacred Ampijoroana falls, where members of the Antakarana community leave offerings for wishes granted. Respect areas marked as sacred (fady) and always follow your guide's instructions.

activities.text: Choose your circuit based on your fitness: the short circuit (2 hours) reaches the small waterfall and Lake Mahasarika, the park's smallest lake, which supplies water to the city of Diego Suarez. The full circuit (5 to 6 hours) climbs to the great waterfall and viewpoints overlooking the Mozambique Channel. Pack waterproof shoes—the forest trails are often slippery.

In the evening at Joffreville, head out on a night walk with your guide. Chameleons and nocturnal lemurs like the rufous mouse lemur are active after dark and far easier to spot with a headlamp. Operators based in Joffreville organize these roughly 1.5-hour outings departing from village accommodations.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Madagascar Road Trip: Tsingy, Three Bays & Nosy Be

places.name: Madirokely

visits.text: Ambanja is the capital of the “valley of perfumes”: the Sambirano Valley produces cocoa, coffee, vanilla, vetiver, and ylang-ylang. If you pass through on a weekday, the local market is worth the detour—spices, tropical fruits, and a 100% local atmosphere. The town's cathedral has a story to tell: its metal framework comes from the former Strasbourg train station. The town is 18 km from Ankify port.

Ankify is the only embarkation point on the northern mainland coast for reaching Nosy Be. A small fishing village, it's above all a transit point. The speedboat to Nosy Be takes 45 minutes. Check schedules in advance—you may have to wait depending on how busy it is. The crossing is generally calm between May and November.

Hell-Ville (Andoany) is the main port and only true town on Nosy Be, named after Admiral Louis de Hell, governor of Réunion, who obtained the island's cession in 1840. At the landing dock, you get your first scent of ylang-ylang drifting through the hot air. Don't linger too long tonight—head to Madirokely, fifteen minutes away, to settle in facing the beach.

Mont Passot rises to 329 meters at Nosy Be's center and offers the island's best panoramic view: eleven volcanic lakes appear below, framed by tropical vegetation, with the ocean on the horizon. Go in late afternoon—it's one of the archipelago's most beautiful sunsets.

The Lokobe Nature Reserve is the last remnant of primary forest on Nosy Be. It protects the black lemur with its black fur, the panther chameleon (Furcifer pardalis) with its shimmering colors, and large trees like Canarium madagascariensis and rosewood. Access is by pirogue from the southeast coast—allow half a day, with a guide required.

The sacred tree of Mahatsinjo, a several-centuries-old Ficus bengalensis with spectacular aerial roots, is a Sakalava worship site. This ancient witness to the island's history can be visited in a few minutes but merits the detour to understand local spirituality.

Nosy Komba, nicknamed “lemur island,” is a volcanic island without roads or cars, 30 minutes by boat from Nosy Be. The village of Ampangorina welcomes visitors with its craft workshops: embroidered tablecloths sewn by hand by village women, rosewood carvings. Don't miss the lemur park—the black-furred macaques are easily approached and live in mixed groups led by females.

Nosy Tanikely became a marine national park in 2010—fishing is prohibited within a 700-meter radius of the lighthouse. The result: an astonishing density of fish right from the beach, well-preserved corals, and seagrass beds where you'll almost certainly encounter green turtles. The interesting underwater scenery starts a few meters from the beach—a beginner with a mask and snorkel sees as much as an experienced diver.

Nosy Sakatia, nicknamed “orchid island,” is a small unspoiled island west of Nosy Be, accessible in 5 minutes by boat from Chanty Beach. Less visited than Tanikely, it charms with its forest trails, wild orchids, and chameleons. Antagnatrozona Bay shelters vast seagrass beds well protected from swells—this is where green turtles come to feed.

Russian Bay, a stopover on the return to Nosy Be, is a sheltered cove on the mainland that still receives very few visitors. The site takes its name from Admiral Rozhestvensky's fleet, which took refuge here in 1905 during the Russo-Japanese War—the camp ruins are still visible. Almost deserted white sand beaches and turtle nests dot the shore.

Hell-Ville (Andoany), 20 minutes from Madirokely, is worth a morning stop before the flight: the central market offers local spices, vanilla, bottled ylang-ylang, and handicrafts. This is where the island's scent is most intense. The colonial waterfront with its old naval cannons and period buildings is also worth a quick stroll.

activities.text: The road between Ankarana and Ankify (about 140 km, 2.5 to 3 hours) first follows the dry forest, then descends toward the coast, passing through Ambilobe and Ambanja. The condition of the RN6 varies on some sections—leave early to have time to see Ambanja before boarding.

The speedboat crossing Ankify → Hell-Ville lasts 45 minutes. If the weather is favorable, you'll spot Nosy Be's verdant coasts long before arriving. Outside the dry season, the sea can be rough—bring a plastic bag if you're prone to seasickness.

Late in the day at Madirokely, enjoy Nosy Be's main beach and unwind after the long drive and sea crossing. It's a wide strip of sand that comes alive in the evening, with beachfront restaurants. You're staying here three nights—get comfortably settled.
Andilana Beach, in the island's north, is Nosy Be's most beautiful: crystal-clear waters, pristine white sand, and few visitors. Plan half a day—allow 45 minutes' drive from Madirokely.
In the evening, stop by Hell-Ville's covered market: local spices, ylang-ylang, vanilla, pepper. It's the best place to pick up fragrant souvenirs from the island of perfumes.

Full-day excursion from Madirokely: Nosy Komba in the morning (lemurs and crafts), Nosy Tanikely in the afternoon (snorkeling). Local operators offer this combination by shared or private boat. You return to Madirokely for the night—no need to move your luggage.

Snorkeling on Nosy Tanikely's reef: the seabed slopes gradually from depths of 2 to 12 meters as you move away from the beach. You'll observe snappers, clownfish, barracudas, giant clams, and green turtles in the seagrass beds. Diadema sea urchins are present—don't touch the bottom.

Morning snorkeling on Nosy Sakatia's seagrass beds: depth of 2 to 3 meters, clear water, green turtles almost guaranteed. Let yourself drift slowly above the seagrass—they'll approach on their own if you remain still. Return to Madirokely early afternoon.
Coastal walk on foot around Nosy Sakatia, from cove to cove: the forest trails cross dense vegetation where wild orchids grow on tree trunks. Bring good shoes—the terrain is uneven.

In the afternoon, prepare for tomorrow's Nosy Iranja expedition: check tide times with your operator (the 1.2 km tombolo is only accessible at low tide), confirm the overnight camp, and pack as lightly as possible for two nights on the island.

Boat trip from Nosy Iranja to Russian Bay (~30 km, 1 hour at sea), hugging the wild mainland coast. A short stopover for a swim or a walk on the deserted beaches, then back north to Nosy Be for the night. Spinner dolphins are common on this route.
Return to Madirokely in the late afternoon—head back to your base hotel and the luggage you left on the island. Last evening on Madirokely Beach before departure.

Final shopping at the Hell-Ville market in the morning, then transfer to Fascene Airport in the east of the island. The airport has scheduled flights to Antananarivo and a few seasonal international connections (Réunion, Addis Ababa, Milan).

visits.text: Morning boat navigation from Akanin'ny Nofy to Tamatave (Toamasina) - about 3 hours on the canal. The city is the great eastern port: its palm-lined avenues and faded colonial houses recall that the east coast long looked toward the Indian Ocean more than the highlands. Stop for a meal at the market before heading north.

Mahambo, 60 km north of Tamatave, is your gateway to Sainte-Marie. Coconut groves, beach exposed to Indian Ocean swells, some waves for surfers. It's simple and honest - use it to rest before the crossing.

activities.text: Swimming or surfing at Mahambo depending on conditions - the east coast is exposed to Indian Ocean swells. Check conditions with your accommodation before jumping in the water.

places.name: Morondava

visits.text: You've seen photos of the Avenue of the Baobabs thousands of times - in real life, it's even more striking. 17 km north of Morondava, a row of Adansonia grandidieri - the most imposing baobab species, endemic to the west coast - raise their silvery trunks 30 m high and 3 m in diameter against a sky that catches fire. These trees are between 300 and 800 years old. Come at sunset - and arrive 30 minutes early to choose your angle.

activities.text: Domestic flight Tuléar → Morondava - check schedules 48 hours before departure. Cross-country connections in Madagascar are notorious for unannounced cancellations. Always have a plan B.

Evening stroll on Nosy Kely beach, Morondava's sandy peninsula - a first contact with the coast after the flight: pirogues pulled up on the sand, fishermen coming home, a slow pace, the opposite of the highlands.

visits.text: Stop at the Maison de l'Isalo, 9 km from Ranohira on the RN7 - it is the best starting point before entering the park. In 45 minutes you grasp the essentials: the massif is made of 250-million-year-old Jurassic sandstone, carved into canyons and needles by erosion. All around you grows the massif's rock-dwelling flora: elephant's-foot pachypodiums, aloes, euphorbias.
Go see the Isalo Window late in the day - this natural arch carved in pink sandstone is the park's iconic sunset spot. Arrive 30 minutes before sunset to secure a good angle and avoid the rush.

Set off early for the Canyon des Makis - the sun heats up fast and lemurs hide after 9am. You'll find seven species here including the ring-tailed maki and Verreaux's sifaka, which dances rather than walks. The canyon is deep, shaded, with dense vegetation at the bottom - a total contrast to the plateau's aridity you just crossed.

The natural pool lies on a separate circuit from the Canyon des Makis, to be planned separately with your guide: a rock basin fed by a waterfall, with cool, clear water. Dive in: after hours of walking under the southern sun, it is the reward. The blue pool, on the Cascade des Nymphes circuit, is tinted a mineral blue-green and is deeper. Check the conditions with your guide.

activities.text: Late afternoon, do a first short 2-hour hike around Ranohira with a guide hired at the park office - mandatory. The golden light on the reliefs at day's end alone justifies the trip.

A big walking day on two separate circuits, each with its own starting point: the Canyon des Makis on one side, and on the other the Namaza circuit, Cascade des Nymphes → black pool → blue pool. Allow 4 to 6 hours depending on your pace, at least 2 liters of water per person, a hat and trekking shoes. It is the best walking day on the whole RN7.

visits.text: Ranomafana means “hot water” in Malagasy - the town had existed since colonial times because of its thermal baths, before the 1986 discovery of a new lemur species changed everything. Patricia Wright, an American primatologist, identified the golden bamboo lemur (Hapalemur aureus) here, a species that feeds almost exclusively on young bamboo shoots containing enough cyanide to kill ten humans. The park created in 1991 to protect this habitat covers 41,600 hectares of tropical rainforest, inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2007.

Enter the park with your compulsory guide first thing in the morning - the lemurs are active early. The Park Centre trail is the most suitable for observing the golden bamboo lemur and Milne-Edwards' sifaka. The park is home to a total of 12 lemur species, 115 bird species and the giraffe weevil - Trachelophorus giraffa - whose disproportionately long neck is a curiosity in its own right.

activities.text: After dinner, take a guided night walk on the edge of Ranomafana Park, beside the RN25: the park's internal trails are not open for night visits. Look for mouse lemurs, chameleons and frogs with your guide. Bring a head torch, long trousers and insect repellent. Book your outing at the park office that morning.
